The foundational premise of somatic feedback posits that all bodily changes are immediately felt, forming a core mapping \( \mathcal{F}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{m} \). This implies a deterministic, continuous relationship between internal neural dynamics and externalized sensation. The emotional sensory complexity \( \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{S}) \) emerges as a composite function of multiple localized signals, weighted by their emotional relevance. The whole body personality field \( \Phi(\mathbf{x}) \) extends this to a spatially distributed, integrative model of selfhood. These primitives form a dual structure: \( \mathcal{F} \) as a forward map, and \( \Phi \) as a reverse integration kernel. Failure modes include sensory masking, where \( \mathcal{F} \) loses injectivity, and emotional ambiguity, where \( \mathcal{C} \) becomes ill-defined. The system exhibits duality through the interplay of local and global perception, with \( \mathcal{F} \) encoding microstates and \( \Phi \) encoding macrostates of identity. The epistemological risk lies in overgeneralizing \( \mathcal{F} \) as linear or static, which violates the dynamic, context-sensitive nature of somatic experience.
